reasons: No automated tests were seen for this file.
The admin password is stored in browser session storage, which is a security weakness.
Chat can show scripted replies that look like real edits when no run exists.
The redirect uses a hardcoded version string that must be updated by hand.
Only 19 of 88 sections (lines 3651 to 4620) were supplied, so most of the file was not reviewed.

terms.meaning: The project database the app reads industries and projects from.
A separate server that runs the analysis and builds the deck outputs.
One attempt by the agent to build a recipe from a chosen set of projects.
A live two-way connection that lets the server push progress updates to the page.
Asking the server for status again and again at set intervals.
Small storage in the browser that is cleared when the tab closes.
The file format used by PowerPoint.
A test-style run that relaxes some release checks, so its output is a draft.
A recorded decision by a reviewer to accept a failed check for internal use.
A short pop-up message shown briefly on screen.

depends_on: Browser features: WebSocket, fetch, session storage

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Redirect to the new lessons tool
sections.what: As soon as the page opens, it sends the visitor to the new lessons-learnt tool, keeping any extra text in the address. The top of the page also loads a shared identity script and sets the page title and build label.
sections.why: The code comment says the old prototype cannot run in a hosted browser, so sending old bookmarks to the production tool keeps them working.
sections.watch_out: The rest of this roughly 4,600-line file was not visible in this packet, so it is unclear whether any of it still runs.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Side rail and button styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the left navigation column, the way it folds down to icons, and the common buttons, small label chips and coloured status tags. A user sees the sidebar, the buttons and the On track, Delayed and Over budget labels.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps one consistent look for navigation and controls across the app.
sections.watch_out: When the rail is folded, labels are hidden through a list of names, so a new label must be added to that list or it will still show.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: Admin, agent and progress panel styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the Analyst and Admin switch, the admin password box, the agent status banner, the run log table, review gate cards, and the progress steps shown while a report is built.
sections.why: Likely reason: groups the back-office and run-tracking looks so they can be changed together.
sections.watch_out: The admin lock is only a visual layer. These styles do not protect anything on their own.

sections.name: File setup (part 4)
sections.title: Home hero and industry tile styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the front page: the large headline, the stats strip, the industry tiles, and the band that invites the user to talk to an expert. It also styles the input boxes in the user panel.
sections.why: Likely reason: the home page is the first screen people see, so its look is set in one place.
sections.watch_out: The industry grid is set to four columns. A responsive rule later in the file changes this on smaller screens, so check both when adding tiles.

sections.name: File setup (part 5)
sections.title: Filter, tab and project card styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the filter row, the tab bar, the headline metric boxes with bars, the lesson list, and the grid of project cards on industry pages.
sections.why: Likely reason: shared look for the list and summary parts of the industry pages.

sections.name: File setup (part 6)
sections.title: Company panel and project page styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the right-hand company list, which opens to show each company's projects, and the project page layout with key facts, lesson blocks, a phase timeline, and a related projects list.
sections.why: Likely reason: supports the expandable company list and the layout of the project page.

sections.name: File setup (part 7)
sections.title: Deck editor and house slide styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the slide editor: the strip of thumbnails on the left, the large preview in the middle, and the slide itself with its title, subtitle and footer. It also styles the branded cover and agenda slides.
sections.why: Likely reason: the preview should look like the final slide, so the slide styles copy the exported design.
sections.watch_out: Thumbnails shrink the full size slide using a scale value set by the script. If that value is missing, a fallback scale is used and thumbnails may look off.

sections.name: File setup (part 8)
sections.title: Slide layouts for steps, pillars and tables
sections.what: Sets the look of the slide types the generator can produce: step columns with chevron headers, pillar columns, a two-column executive view, data tables, large metric numbers, bullet lists, speaker notes, and the floating toolbar on the slide canvas.
sections.why: Likely reason: one set of layout rules for each slide type keeps generated decks uniform.

sections.name: File setup (part 9)
sections.title: AI chat panel and reading view styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the assistant chat panel where users type requests to change a deck, the reading view that shows the deck as a document, and the empty-state message shown when there is nothing to display.
sections.why: Likely reason: the assistant and reading view have their own look, separate from the slides.

sections.name: File setup (part 10)
sections.title: Expert page, deck filters and pop-up styles
sections.what: Sets the look of the Talk to an Expert page with its side panel and disclaimer box, the deck filter controls, expert cards with an online status dot, and the short pop-up messages that confirm an action.
sections.why: Likely reason: groups the expert directory, the filter sidebar, and the shared pop-up message style.

sections.name: File setup (part 11)
sections.title: Keyboard focus, motion and page shell
sections.what: Adds a visible outline when a user tabs to a control, turns off animation for users who ask their system to reduce motion, and adjusts column widths on narrower screens. It then starts the page structure with the side rail, its header and collapse button, and the industry list.
sections.why: Likely reason: keyboard focus and reduced motion are accessibility support, and the narrow-screen rule keeps layout usable.
sections.watch_out: The reduced motion rule applies to every element, so any behaviour that relies on animation may jump instead of animating.

sections.name: File setup (part 12)
sections.title: Page sections and admin password box
sections.what: Lays out the main area as one section per page: home, industry, project, company, deck, admin and experts. The home section holds the headline, stats, industry tiles and expert call to action. A password box for the admin view is also here, and it shows a default placeholder password on screen.
sections.why: Likely reason: each page is a hidden section that the script shows when the user navigates, and the password box guards the admin view.
sections.watch_out: The default admin password is written into the page and displayed to the user, so the lock is not real security. The default must be changed before any shared use.

sections.name: File setup (part 13)
sections.title: Built-in industry names and app data holders
sections.what: Holds the fixed list of industries with their names, taglines and colours, plus empty holders for industries, projects and companies. Project data is filled in later from the server, and the lists stay empty if the server does not respond.
sections.why: Likely reason: industry labels and colours are set once here, while project data is loaded at startup.
sections.watch_out: Projects are only shown when the server supplies them, so a server outage shows empty lists rather than sample data.

sections.name: File setup (part 14)
sections.title: App memory and agent address
sections.what: Holds the app's working memory: current page, chosen industry, deck choices, filters, theme and chat history. It also works out the address of the local research agent and saves that address in the browser.
sections.why: Likely reason: one shared memory object lets every screen read the same choices.
sections.watch_out: The agent address is stored in the browser, so an old saved address can keep pointing at a wrong port until the code repairs it.

sections.name: File setup (part 15)
sections.title: Restoring the last report run
sections.what: When the page opens, it looks for the most recent report run the user had and reloads it so their work comes back. Opening the page with the new flag starts fresh instead. It also reads the run's chosen industry back into the app.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the user's place after a refresh or a return visit.
sections.watch_out: Errors during restore are silently ignored and the run is forgotten, so a missing report can look like a lost one.

sections.name: File setup (part 16)
sections.title: Agent status check and English polishing
sections.what: Asks the agent whether it is running and which features it has. It also provides the Re-enhance English action, which runs a language polishing step on the report and shows a short message with the result.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the user check whether the optional writing helper works before relying on it.
sections.watch_out: When polishing does not use the language model, the message points to a missing key but gives only a short status word, so the cause may be unclear.

sections.name: File setup (part 17)
sections.title: Colour themes and custom colours
sections.what: Defines the built-in colour themes, hides the beacon theme from the analyst list, and applies the chosen colours to the page and to every branded slide. Custom colours chosen by the user override the theme colours.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fallback list of themes is kept so the app still works if the server does not return its own.
sections.watch_out: Custom colours are saved in the browser and override the theme on each load, so a theme change may seem to do nothing.

sections.name: File setup (part 18)
sections.title: Colour helpers for slides
sections.what: Small helpers that mix and lighten colours and pick a banner, background and accent colour for each slide based on its type. They also build the style text that sets slide colours.
sections.why: Likely reason: each slide type gets its own colour role so the deck reads consistently.
sections.watch_out: Slide types that are not listed fall back to alternating colours by position, so a new slide type may look inconsistent until it is added to the list.

sections.name: File setup (part 19)
sections.title: Fonts and saving colour choices
sections.what: Loads a Google font when a slide font is chosen, applies it to the slides, reads the custom colour picker values, and packages the theme choices so they can be sent to the server.
sections.why: Likely reason: Google fonts are loaded only when needed, which keeps the page light.
sections.watch_out: Fonts load from an outside Google address, so slides fall back to a default font when the machine is offline.

sections.name: File setup (part 20)
sections.title: Helpers and project matching rules
sections.what: Gives the app basic helpers: a shortcut for finding page elements, an escape step that makes text safe to show on screen, and labels for statuses. It also holds the trait presets, the text search rule, and the rules that decide whether a project matches the base filters.
sections.why: Likely reason: the escape helper stops project text from being read as page markup when it is shown.
sections.watch_out: The foak trait is guessed from words such as prototype or SMR in the project text, so it can match loosely.

sections.name: File setup (part 21)
sections.title: Example name filter and industry choice
sections.what: Narrows the project list by typed example names and adds projects that share a place or technology with them. It also switches the deck to another industry and works out which industry is currently selected.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets an analyst build a deck around specific projects and their close peers.
sections.watch_out: When example names match nothing in the filtered results, the code widens the search to all matching names, so the result can be broader than the filters suggest.

sections.name: File setup (part 22)
sections.title: Project lists and filter counts
sections.what: Collects the projects in the chosen industry, reports how many match the filters and how many are in the deck, and refreshes those count labels. It updates the labels without rebuilding the filter boxes, so typing does not lose focus.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the counts current while the user types into the filter boxes.
sections.watch_out: The source list under the filters is rebuilt during refresh, so its contents can change while the user is looking at it.

sections.name: File setup (part 23)
sections.title: Turning filters into an agent request
sections.what: Converts the filter bar choices into the search terms sent to the research agent when a report is generated. Typed example names take priority. If none are typed, the matched project names are sent, but only when there are 200 or fewer.
sections.why: Likely reason: so the report follows the filter bar rather than the whole project database.
sections.watch_out: Above 200 matches, the project names are not sent, so the agent may search more widely than the filter bar shows. Other filters still apply.

sections.name: File setup (part 24)
sections.title: Deck filter panel and reader
sections.what: Builds the search and filter panel for the deck, with fields for status, geography, technology, company, delivery model, minimum capex, and example project names, plus trait buttons and a clear button. A second helper reads the typed values back from the page into the saved filter settings, so the filters survive redraws.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the user narrow which projects feed the Generate Recipe step. Reason not stated in the code for the compact option that hides some fields.
sections.watch_out: The example projects box expects exact project names from the agent database, so a small spelling difference silently matches nothing.

sections.name: File setup (part 25)
sections.title: Shared small helpers and sidebar list
sections.what: Provides the two-letter initials used for company badges, the small pop-up messages that appear for a few seconds, the Industry, Methodology, PPTX and Manuscript tab switcher, and the add-to-deck button. It also starts drawing the industry list in the sidebar with project counts.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. These are reused across several pages, so they are kept as shared helpers.
sections.watch_out: The Manuscript link only works after a run exists; before that it is a disabled button, so users may think the feature is broken.

sections.name: File setup (part 26)
sections.title: Home page and industry page header
sections.what: Finishes the sidebar list, which highlights the current role. Draws the home page with summary numbers and one card per industry, showing a loading or sign-in message when no industry data is present. Begins the industry page with its breadcrumb, title, tagline, add-to-deck button, and the Snapshot and Projects tabs.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The home page message changes depending on whether data has loaded.
sections.watch_out: The home page empty message depends on a single loaded flag, so a failed load can look the same as a slow one.

sections.name: File setup (part 27)
sections.title: Industry snapshot, project cards and company list
sections.what: Shows either the snapshot view or a grid of project cards, with a message when the status filter hides everything. Adds a side panel listing companies that can expand to show their projects. The snapshot view shows a fixed summary paragraph, capital split by segment, four top lessons, and four headline numbers.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The snapshot is built from the industry summary data, so the page is one view over the same data.
sections.watch_out: The summary paragraph is fixed wording that is written into every industry page, so it can claim a pattern the real data does not show.

sections.name: File setup (part 28)
sections.title: Project page data fallbacks
sections.what: Works out what the project page shows when the data is incomplete. It builds a timeline from start, lifecycle, completion and delay values, falls back to a single status line if none exist, lists owner, developer and contractor, and chooses lessons from stored lessons, then from evidence facts, then from basic overview fields. It also starts drawing the project page header.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The fallbacks let a project with sparse records still show a usable page.
sections.watch_out: Placeholder text such as dashes or n.d. is treated as missing in some places but not others, so a missing date may appear as an odd value.

sections.name: File setup (part 29)
sections.title: Project page content
sections.what: Draws the project page body: overview, key lessons, delivery timeline, an at-a-glance fact list, stakeholders, and a related projects list. Stakeholder names become links only when they match a known company. Related projects are picked by shared owner, route or country, and if none match, other projects in the same industry are shown.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Linking names to company pages lets users move between projects and companies.
sections.watch_out: When no related project matches, the list silently shows unrelated projects from the same industry, which can look like a real relationship.

sections.name: File setup (part 30)
sections.title: Company page totals and layout
sections.what: Adds up each company's planned capital across its projects (falling back to actual capital) and shows it in billions or millions. It counts on-track projects and delayed or over-budget projects, and lists process routes and countries. The company page then shows four headline cells, an overview paragraph, and the company's project cards.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The totals give a quick summary of each company's portfolio.
sections.watch_out: The total mixes planned and actual figures from different projects, so the number is not a clean spend total even though the page calls it capital tracked.

sections.name: File setup (part 31)
sections.title: Deck outcome labels and pillar builder
sections.what: Labels each project as Delivered, Overran, Cautionary, or In progress from its status and completion text. The pillar builder groups all evidence facts by category, keeps the eight categories with the most facts, and creates the cover, executive summary, agenda, and framework slides. If there are no facts, it uses one placeholder pillar.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the deck's main themes come from the evidence itself rather than a fixed template, as the code comments suggest.
sections.watch_out: Categories beyond the top eight are dropped without any notice, so a small but important theme can vanish from the deck.

sections.name: File setup (part 32)
sections.title: Evidence slides and Yard slide conversion
sections.what: Creates one slide per pillar with up to five evidence lines and up to three source links, then an assessment slide that repeats the top pillars, the first three project lessons, and a fixed closing recommendation. It also starts converting slides returned by the Yard service into the page's own format.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The closing recommendation is a fixed line that applies to every deck.
sections.watch_out: Project names are cut at the first opening bracket, so names that contain brackets lose their second half on these slides.

sections.name: File setup (part 33)
sections.title: Pillar evidence and slide labels
sections.what: For pillar slides from the Yard service, adds evidence excerpts when the slide has none, matched by pillar id or title. It then sets section labels such as Executive Summary, Pillar, and Assessment, and returns the converted slides. If no Yard slides exist yet, the page uses the placeholder slides instead.
sections.why: The code comment says the official preview must come from Yard's Recipe output, so placeholders are only a stand-in.
sections.watch_out: Pillars are matched by title text as a fallback, so two pillars with similar names could receive each other's evidence.

sections.name: File setup (part 34)
sections.title: Placeholder slides before generation
sections.what: Creates simple placeholder slides for industry, project, and deck pages before a Recipe has been generated, using the words Generate Recipe to explain what is missing. It also starts the function that draws each slide, with a footer that uses the brand name from the shared identity settings and the layouts for cover, center note, agenda, and executive summary.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the slide area useful before any real run exists.
sections.watch_out: The project placeholder reads the industry name directly, so a project whose industry is not in the list will cause an error.

sections.name: File setup (part 35)
sections.title: Slide layouts for overview, pillars and tables
sections.what: Continues the slide drawing code with layouts for the overview chevrons, pillar slides with a coloured banner, principle, narrative, good and bad notes, and columns of points, and table layouts for project directory and chart data sheets.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each slide type has its own layout so the output looks like a formal consulting deck.
sections.watch_out: The pillar number shown in the banner is read from the title text, so a title without a number shows 1.

sections.name: File setup (part 36)
sections.title: Slide layouts for charts and scorecards
sections.what: Continues with layouts for the scoring criteria table, the project universe and geography columns, bar charts, the coloured heatmap grid with a legend, and the start of the findings list.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Each layout turns the same stored data into a different visual.
sections.watch_out: Colour values from the stored data are placed straight into the page styling, so a malformed colour value will display incorrectly.

sections.name: File setup (part 37)
sections.title: Bubble chart, case profiles and default slide
sections.what: Finishes the findings list, then draws the cost against schedule bubble chart with a dot for each project. Builds case profile slides in split, key information only, or pillar only layouts depending on which data exists, then draws the scorecard table and a standard bullet slide used for everything else.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The layouts adapt to whatever information is available for each project.
sections.watch_out: The bubble chart shows at most 40 projects and scales its axes to the data, so a single extreme project compresses all the others.

sections.name: File setup (part 38)
sections.title: Thumbnails and deck editor
sections.what: Draws the small preview thumbnails and sizes them to fit. Builds the deck editor, which contains the slide strip, the main preview, and buttons for Download pptx when a run is live or Generate Recipe when not, plus the Admin button and the assistant panel. An add slide button appears only before a run exists.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The editor switches its buttons depending on whether a live run exists.
sections.watch_out: The download button only appears for a live run, so users with a draft preview will not see a way to download a file.

sections.name: File setup (part 39)
sections.title: Turning a finished run into slides
sections.what: Converts the stored result of a finished run into the full slide set: cover, executive summary, agenda, overview, and one slide per pillar showing up to four sub-drivers with trimmed text. It uses the wording from the run where it exists and falls back to fixed wording otherwise.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the page showing the same story as the downloaded deck. Reason not stated in the code for the trimming length.
sections.watch_out: The cover title falls back to a fixed phrase about delivering megaprojects, which will appear even for other industries if the run gives no title.

sections.name: File setup (part 40)
sections.title: Project directory and geography slides
sections.what: Finishes the pillar slides. Builds the project universe slide that groups projects into delivered, overran or cautionary, and in progress, then builds a project directory with up to nine rows shown from up to thirty-six projects. Starts grouping projects by geography.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Grouping by outcome and location lets a reader see the whole project set at a glance.
sections.watch_out: Any outcome that is not Delivered, Overran, or Cautionary is counted as in progress, so an unusual label will be placed in the wrong group.

sections.name: File setup (part 41)
sections.title: Geography, heatmap, bubble and case profiles
sections.what: Builds the geography slide with up to eight regions, the heatmap of projects against pillars with up to eighteen rows, and the bubble data. Starts building one case profile slide for each of the first ten projects.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. These are the chart slides that turn the scorecard into visuals.
sections.watch_out: When a project has no overrun figures, the bubble chart places it at an invented position based on its outcome, so that dot does not show real data.

sections.name: File setup (part 42)
sections.title: Case profile content, appendix and closing slides
sections.what: Builds the key facts and pillar takeaways for each case profile, labels each project as Success Story, Cautionary Tale, Mixed Success, or To be Determined, and skips projects with no facts. Adds an appendix fact register with up to eight entries and any extra closing or centre slides chosen in the deck settings. Assigns colours to each slide and starts loading the run result.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The verdict labels give readers a quick reading of each case.
sections.watch_out: The verdict mapping is not symmetrical, since Cautionary outcomes are labelled Mixed Success while Overran outcomes are labelled Cautionary Tale, which can confuse readers comparing them.

sections.name: File setup (part 43)
sections.title: Loading a finished run and downloading the file
sections.what: Loads a finished run's result, stores it, and refreshes the slides. Asks the server to render the PowerPoint file using the chosen theme and then reloads the preview. Downloads the rendered file and saves it as recipe.pptx.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Rendering on the server means the downloaded file matches what the preview shows.
sections.watch_out: The download always uses the same file name, so repeated downloads may overwrite or duplicate an earlier copy on the user's computer.

sections.name: File setup (part 44)
sections.title: Loading slides and applying theme
sections.what: Asks the agent service for slides using the chosen theme, colours, and font, applies those settings, and redraws the preview. Adds slide kind and colour data to each slide that arrives without them. An override route can also be requested for analyst changes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The preview uses the service's theme so that screen and file match.
sections.watch_out: Any failure returns nothing without a message, so the page can quietly keep an older preview and the user may not notice the update did not happen.

sections.name: File setup (part 45)
sections.title: Live preview overlay and draft slides
sections.what: Copies the run result and overlays the industry name, the user's prompt, and the selection size, either all matching projects or the first N up to 500. Before any run exists, builds draft slides from the inputs, using placeholder pillars whose names change when the prompt mentions certain keywords.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the user see how their choices change the deck before spending time generating it.
sections.watch_out: When the selection size field is missing, the code uses a fixed value of 136 and the default industry is a fixed Lithium Mining name, so these can appear without the user choosing them.

sections.name: File setup (part 46)
sections.title: Simple chat commands for the preview
sections.what: Reads short chat messages and applies them to the preview copy: renaming a pillar, setting the thesis or a pillar's principle, showing or hiding the run ID on the cover, and adding a centre slide. Any longer message that does not match a command becomes the thesis on the cover.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the user change the deck quickly by typing, and mirrors commands the agent service also understands.
sections.watch_out: Any message over 24 characters that matches no command replaces the thesis in the preview, so a typed question can overwrite the real thesis on the cover.

sections.name: File setup (part 47)
sections.title: Live preview rebuild from prompt and chat
sections.what: Rebuilds the deck preview as the user types a prompt or a chat message. If a full server-built deck is already loaded, it edits titles, the cover subtitle, the first executive bullet and pillar names in place. Chat lines such as rename pillar, set thesis, remove the run id or add a centre slide are read with pattern matching. If no full deck exists, it rebuilds from the base canonical data or from the current inputs.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the preview responsive while typing, without asking the server to regenerate the whole deck each time.
sections.watch_out: Chat commands are matched by pattern, so a small wording change or typo fails silently and nothing visible happens.

sections.name: File setup (part 48)
sections.title: Chat edits and deck strip repaint
sections.what: Applies the last chat-driven edits to the slide list and then redraws the slide thumbnail strip and the large slide view. The strip label shows live when a server run exists and draft otherwise. If the expected page elements are missing, it falls back to a full deck redraw.
sections.why: Likely reason: redraws only the preview area so the chat box keeps focus while the user types.
sections.watch_out: The fallback full redraw can reset what the user has typed unless the prompt value is restored, which only the debounced update path does.

sections.name: File setup (part 49)
sections.title: Debounced preview update and chat panel
sections.what: Waits about 180 milliseconds after the last keystroke before refreshing the preview. On the deck page it switches the view to the PPTX editor automatically. It also builds the Deck Assistant chat panel, including suggestion buttons that change depending on whether a live run and free-form chat are available.
sections.why: Likely reason: the short wait avoids a refresh on every keystroke, and the automatic switch lets the user see live changes right away.
sections.watch_out: The automatic switch to the PPTX view can surprise a user who was looking at another deck view while typing.

sections.name: File setup (part 50)
sections.title: Deck builder page header and PPTX branch
sections.what: Builds the top bar of the Deck Builder page with the Generate Recipe button and the Download PPTX and Download Manuscript buttons. Those download buttons are disabled until a run exists. For the PPTX view it then shows one of three states: a progress message while the run is busy, a halt message when the run stopped, or the live slide editor.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page must show progress or halt messages instead of a blank or stale slide, so the state is checked before the editor is drawn.
sections.watch_out: While a run is busy this code clears the stored slides on purpose, so any unsaved slide edits in the preview are lost.

sections.name: File setup (part 51)
sections.title: Deck page layout, methodology and sources
sections.what: Finishes the Deck page. It shows a prompt when no slides exist yet, a methodology view when that tab is chosen, and otherwise a two-column layout with a sources list on the left and the recipe HTML in an embedded frame on the right. It also shows loading or empty messages where the recipe output is not yet available.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page has several stages (empty, busy, finished, loading outputs) and each needs its own message.
sections.watch_out: One long empty-state sentence in the sources area is cut off in the file listing, so its exact wording could not be confirmed here.

sections.name: File setup (part 52)
sections.title: Project checkboxes, reading view and experts
sections.what: Lists each project inside an industry with a checkbox and a Select visible or Clear visible button. The reading view on the Deck page shows a written summary of lessons from the chosen projects, grouped by industry. The Talk to an Expert page is a placeholder that says no experts are loaded.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code for the expert placeholder. The page text says the directory is not yet connected to the Yard project data.
sections.watch_out: The reading view's opening sentence is fixed wording inside the code, so editing the data will not change it.

sections.name: File setup (part 53)
sections.title: Page navigation and admin lock
sections.what: Switches the visible page and remembers the last Deck or Home page in browser storage. It also remembers whether the admin area has been unlocked for the current browser session and shows or hides the password prompt.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app keeps the user on the same page after a reload and keeps admin access until the browser session ends.
sections.watch_out: The unlock flag lives only in the browser, so it is a convenience check and not real protection for admin actions on the server.

sections.name: File setup (part 54)
sections.title: Role switching and admin login
sections.what: Switches between the analyst and admin roles. Choosing admin opens the password prompt unless the browser is already unlocked. The login sends the password to the agent's login endpoint and shows an error if it is refused. It also defines the list of pipeline stages and the coarse progress phases shown to users.
sections.why: Likely reason: analysts should see only the simple progress view, while admins can see the detail behind the pipeline.
sections.watch_out: The password is also saved in browser session storage in plain text, so anyone with access to that browser session can read it.

sections.name: File setup (part 55)
sections.title: Plain-language halt and mode labels
sections.what: Turns the agent's internal halt messages into short sentences an analyst can act on, such as telling them to loosen filters. It also chooses the Pristine or Smoke badge shown next to a run, with a tooltip explaining why.
sections.why: Likely reason: raw halt reasons are technical, so this code maps the common ones to plain advice.
sections.watch_out: The messages are matched by keywords in the halt text, so if the backend rewords a halt reason the analyst gets a generic message.

sections.name: File setup (part 56)
sections.title: Run status strip and override panel start
sections.what: Draws the strip that shows the current run status, the mode badge, and every pipeline stage as a coloured pill. It also starts the override panel shown when a run has halted. The panel lists the failed checks as blockers, marking the critical ones separately.
sections.why: Likely reason: analysts need to see at a glance where a run stopped and which checks blocked it.
sections.watch_out: Critical versus quality severity is decided by a fixed list of check names, so a renamed check will be shown with the wrong severity.

sections.name: File setup (part 57)
sections.title: Override form and progress display
sections.what: Finishes the override panel. It shows counts of critical and quality blockers, one checkbox per blocker, an acknowledgement box, and a reason field. It also builds the progress view that combines run status, the phase steps, the quality coach and the English enhancer.
sections.why: Likely reason: the analyst must accept each failed check on purpose before the run continues, so the form asks for an explicit acknowledgement and reason.
sections.watch_out: The panel says earlier waivers stay visible, so a user may think waived checks no longer count, but they still block release qualification.

sections.name: File setup (part 58)
sections.title: Quality coach and English enhancer panels
sections.what: Shows the quality coach's headline, its top suggestions, research targets and learning hints. It also shows the status of the English enhancer, which writes the analysis text, and a Re-enhance English button.
sections.why: Likely reason: users need to know whether the wording comes from the language model or from a simple fallback.
sections.watch_out: When no Portkey key is set, the note tells the user to edit a settings file, so a missing key looks like a setup problem rather than a fallback.

sections.name: File setup (part 59)
sections.title: Recipe input form and colour pickers
sections.what: Draws the Generate Recipe input form. It has the industry name, a project count or All matching toggle, theme and font choices, an optional prompt, and colour pickers for accent, navy, ink and wash. It also shows the current filter match count.
sections.why: Likely reason: these are the choices the recipe run needs before it can build the deck.
sections.watch_out: The fallback industry name Lithium Mining and the fallback count of 136 are fixed in the code, so an empty form can quietly target the wrong scope.

sections.name: File setup (part 60)
sections.title: Download buttons and review prompt
sections.what: Shows buttons for opening the HTML, the methodology, the PPTX view and the manuscript once they exist. It also shows the feedback prompt that opens the human review area as soon as outputs are ready, without waiting for the grader. The admin state track at the end of this section shows the run's stages.
sections.why: Likely reason: human review is opened early so reviewers do not have to wait for the automated grader.
sections.watch_out: Some buttons appear only when specific output ids are present, so a missing output looks like a bug when the run has really stopped before that step.

sections.name: File setup (part 61)
sections.title: Grader scores card
sections.what: Shows the automated grader's score table with pass, warn and fail labels, the suggested corrections, the grader memory notes and a status line about the language model coach. Before grading finishes it shows a short waiting message.
sections.why: Likely reason: the grader runs after the outputs are made, so the card explains when a grade is still pending.
sections.watch_out: The card reads only the first few entries of each list, so long lists are shortened on screen.

sections.name: File setup (part 62)
sections.title: Human review and timing cards
sections.what: The Human review card has a notes box, a Save findings button, an Approve latest button, the history of past feedback and the list of config versions. The Efficiency card shows expected versus actual time for each stage, with a flag where the time ran over.
sections.why: Likely reason: the review card lets an analyst feed corrections back into the rules, and the efficiency card helps spot slow stages.
sections.watch_out: Approving feedback writes changes back to the gate and rubric settings according to the page text, so it can change how later runs are judged.

sections.name: File setup (part 63)
sections.title: Golden deltas and saved state rows
sections.what: Builds the Golden deltas card, which compares each metric against a reference result and marks differences. It then starts the Durable state table, which lists each saved checkpoint, its timestamp and its payload file name, one row per pipeline stage.
sections.why: Likely reason: the golden comparison shows whether results have drifted from a known good run.
sections.watch_out: The table row is built across this section and the next, so a reader looking at only one part will not see the full row.

sections.name: File setup (part 64)
sections.title: Saved state rows and test harness card
sections.what: Finishes the durable state rows, showing the recipe lines and analysis digest saved at each checkpoint, and closes the table. It then starts the POPPY harness card, which shows the run mode and a results table of pass or fail checks, with soft passes marked in red.
sections.why: Likely reason: the saved checkpoints let a crashed run resume, and the harness card shows the automated test results for each run.
sections.watch_out: Soft passes are drawn in the same red style as failures, so a user may read a passing check as a failure.

sections.name: File setup (part 65)
sections.title: Harness details and admin page setup
sections.what: Finishes the harness card with the regression counts (fixed, still failing, new) and the stage trace. It then starts the Admin page: it checks the lock, builds the header buttons, the status banner and the summary cards, and draws the gate cards for gates A to C, with gate D hidden until it is used.
sections.why: Likely reason: gate D appears only when that gate is actually used, so the page is not cluttered with an empty gate.
sections.watch_out: A missing gate D card is intended, not a sign that a gate result was lost.

sections.name: File setup (part 66)
sections.title: Admin artifact links and auth switch
sections.what: Adds the links to each output file on the Admin page and a link to the analysis data when it exists. It then starts the recipe section, which includes a constant named AUTH_DISABLED. When that constant is true, every request uses a fixed placeholder token instead of a real sign-in token. The section also builds the scope and project list sent with each recipe request.
sections.why: The code comment says the switch is temporary and must be reverted with the app-wide auth settings. The reason it is on is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: With AUTH_DISABLED set to true, the app does not check who is calling, so it must be turned back off before real use.

sections.name: File setup (part 67)
sections.title: Build request and preview refresh
sections.what: Builds the request body that tells the agent which projects to use, taking the picked projects first, then the active filters, and otherwise the whole industry. It also applies a returned recipe to the preview and fetches a fresh preview on request, reporting the pillars in the chat.
sections.why: Likely reason: the request uses the same project selection rules as the export, so the preview matches what the deck will contain.
sections.watch_out: The schedule function for preview refresh does nothing except clear a timer, so any code that expects it to refresh the preview will be ignored.

sections.name: File setup (part 68)
sections.title: Loading run results into the page
sections.what: Fetches the run details from the agent and stores them. For a halted run it loads the override details. For a finished run it sets the links for the HTML, methodology and PPTX outputs, and loads the canonical data when available. Any error returns nothing and does not show a message.
sections.why: Likely reason: timestamps are added to some links so the browser does not show an old cached file.
sections.watch_out: Errors are swallowed without a message, so a failed fetch looks like a run with no outputs and gives the user no clue why.

sections.name: File setup (part 69)
sections.title: Sending halt override to the agent
sections.what: Checks that the acknowledgement box is ticked, the reason has at least 10 characters, and at least one failed check is selected. It then sends the waiver to the agent's override endpoint, shows the result in the chat, and starts watching the continued run. Busy and error states are reset when it finishes.
sections.why: Likely reason: the checks stop an analyst from waiving problems by accident or without a stated reason.
sections.watch_out: The actor name is fixed as Beacon analyst, so the saved record does not show which person approved the waiver.

sections.name: File setup (part 70)
sections.title: Monitor re-run and begin recipe setup
sections.what: The first part checks a re-run every second for up to five minutes and refreshes the deck and admin screens. The second part, the start of Generate Recipe, confirms the agent server is reachable and copies the screen settings into memory.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: If a run takes longer than five minutes, the monitor shows a 'still running' error while the run keeps going on the server.

sections.name: File setup (part 71)
sections.title: Pick projects and check filters
sections.what: Counts the projects that match the active filters and stops with a message if none match. It then tries to fetch the matching project set from the Yard and builds the settings for the new run.
sections.why: Likely reason: the Yard export is preferred so the recipe uses the same project set the user sees on screen.
sections.watch_out: The Yard export and the filters are both used to choose projects, so a filter change may not reach the run if the export succeeds.

sections.name: File setup (part 72)
sections.title: Fall back to agent database and create run
sections.what: If the Yard export fails or the user is not signed in, the app switches to the agent's own pilot database and shows a notice. It then builds the run request (industry, number of projects, filters, theme, run mode) and sends it to create a new run.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps Generate working when the Yard is unavailable.
sections.watch_out: The run mode is set to smoke, which relaxes some release checks, so the output should be treated as a labelled draft.

sections.name: File setup (part 73)
sections.title: Listen for live progress updates
sections.what: Opens a live connection to the run and adds progress events and phase changes to the admin view as they arrive. It closes when the run succeeds or halts, or after three minutes.
sections.why: Likely reason: progress appears without repeated server requests, with polling as the backup.
sections.watch_out: If the connection fails silently, the screen relies on polling, so progress can look stale for a while.

sections.name: File setup (part 74)
sections.title: Poll run status and load outputs
sections.what: Checks the run status every second for up to two minutes and reports the current phase. On a halt it shows the reason and loads any analyst override. On success it sets the links for the HTML, PDF and PowerPoint outputs and asks the server to re-render the slides with the current theme.
sections.why: Likely reason: polling covers cases where the live connection misses the finish.
sections.watch_out: The loop stops after 120 checks, so a slow run can end the wait while still running; the status is then read once more.

sections.name: File setup (part 75)
sections.title: Final recipe message and empty-run test
sections.what: Writes a chat message saying whether the analysis used the language model, a fallback draft, or plain outputs, and points to the Methodology tab. It also contains a test helper, agentStartEmptyGateB, which starts a run that filters out every project to check the halt behaviour.
sections.why: Likely reason: the test helper checks that the app handles a run with no projects without crashing. Reason for the chat wording not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The test helper sends degraded_verify set to true, which skips some verification, so it should not be reachable from normal use.

sections.name: File setup (part 76)
sections.title: Resume a stopped run and refresh
sections.what: agentResume asks the server to resume the current run and waits up to about thirty seconds for it to finish, then loads the results. agentRefresh reloads the current run's outputs and redraws the screens. presentPptx switches the deck view to PowerPoint and loads its data.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: agentResume gives up after about thirty seconds, so a long run can appear finished while it is still going.

sections.name: File setup (part 77)
sections.title: Click handler for special buttons
sections.what: Listens for clicks across the page, checks which special button attribute was clicked, and runs the matching action. This part covers applying theme colours, downloading a fresh PowerPoint, running an analyst override, toggling deck filters, and similar actions.
sections.why: Likely reason: one shared listener is simpler than attaching a handler to each button.
sections.watch_out: A new button type probably needs its attribute added both to the list at the top of this handler and to the matching branch, or its clicks will do nothing.

sections.name: File setup (part 78)
sections.title: Deck filters, selection and feedback saving
sections.what: Handles clicks for deck filter chips and clearing, selecting all filtered projects, sending a chat edit, and saving reviewer findings to the server. Saving findings needs the admin password, which is read from session storage and sent in a request header.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The admin password sits in browser session storage, so anyone using that browser session can read it.

sections.name: File setup (part 79)
sections.title: Approve write-backs and nav buttons
sections.what: Completes an approval by applying the chosen write-back, then refreshes the admin view. It also handles simple buttons for the rail toggle, role switch, admin lock, refresh, recipe, present and navigation.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Approval uses the same stored admin password as findings saving, so the same exposure applies.

sections.name: File setup (part 80)
sections.title: Route clicks to pages and deck
sections.what: Handles clicks that open an industry, project or company page, switch views, cycle or clear status filters, add or remove projects from the deck, and move between slides. Each click updates the in-memory state and redraws the matching page.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Project and company lookups need the lists to be loaded first; a click before that shows a 'not loaded' message.

sections.name: File setup (part 81)
sections.title: Keyboard, typing and filter input events
sections.what: Handles Enter to send chat, Escape to close the admin unlock box, growing the chat box as text is typed, live preview updates, and filter counts that refresh after a short pause.
sections.why: Likely reason: the preview and counts stay current as the user types, without a button press.
sections.watch_out: Filter counts wait about 80 milliseconds before refreshing, so they can lag briefly behind typing.

sections.name: File setup (part 82)
sections.title: Change industry, selection and count inputs
sections.what: Changing the industry name updates the active industry and redraws the side rail. Changing the project count switches to selecting the first N projects and clears the select-all tick. Both end with a live preview refresh.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Typing an industry name overwrites the active industry in shared state, which can change what Generate uses.

sections.name: File setup (part 83)
sections.title: Send chat messages to the deck assistant
sections.what: Sends typed messages to the live agent chat when a successful run with a recipe exists, then updates the deck and preview and shows the reply. With a run but no recipe it shows a helpful note. With no run at all it returns a fixed scripted reply.
sections.why: Likely reason: scripted replies let the demo look responsive when no real run exists.
sections.watch_out: Scripted replies describe edits such as 'regrouped the lessons' that never happen, so they can mislead a user.

sections.name: File setup (part 84)
sections.title: Format money and build project rows
sections.what: Converts raw Yard project data into the shape the screens use: cost text in millions or billions, a status word (on track, delayed, over budget), dates, location and capacity. It keeps planned and actual amounts so totals can be added up.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Status is worked out from words in the status text and from delay months above six, so a label reflects these rules rather than the source's own status.

sections.name: File setup (part 85)
sections.title: Group projects by operator and technology
sections.what: buildCompanies groups projects under their operator, with unnamed operators placed in one group. buildSegments counts projects per technology and keeps the top eight. The section also contains the start of the Yard data loader.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: buildCompanies keeps only the first 60 operators, so the rest are dropped without any warning.

sections.name: File setup (part 86)
sections.title: Load each industry and summarise stats
sections.what: Loops over each industry, fetches its projects from the Yard, and builds its stats: project count, total capital, company count, on-time share and over-budget share. An industry that fails is skipped with a console warning, and an authorisation failure stops the whole load.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: A failed industry is skipped with only a console warning, so it can look like missing data rather than a load error.

sections.name: File setup (part 87)
sections.title: Admin lock form and window resize
sections.what: Sets up the admin unlock box. Clicking outside it or Cancel returns the user to the analyst role. Submitting the password calls the unlock routine and shows an error if it fails. A window resize also redraws the slide thumbnails.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The unlock relies on tryAdminUnlock, which is not in the supplied lines, so the strength of the admin check cannot be judged here.

sections.name: File setup (part 88)
sections.title: Page startup and Yard connection
sections.what: On load, it draws the home screen, loads themes and agent settings, and checks sign-in. Without a sign-in token it redirects to the login page. With a token it loads industries from the Yard, restores the last agent run, opens the last page and shows a status notice.
sections.why: Likely reason: the screens need Yard data before they can show projects, so the startup waits for it.
sections.watch_out: The login redirect contains a hardcoded version string, so a new release must update it or users may see an old cached page.

summary: The main Beacon web page, where a user builds a lessons-learned deck from Yard project data and an analysis agent's runs, and chats with a deck assistant.
purpose: Lets a signed-in user pick projects, generate a lessons-learned recipe (a set of HTML, PDF and PowerPoint outputs), watch the run's progress, review the results, and make edits. It also has an admin area for reviewing and approving feedback.
why: Likely reason: the app keeps the whole interface in one page so it can update the screen in place without reloading. Reason for the single-file layout not stated in the code.
how: 1. On load, it draws the home screen and checks sign-in; without sign-in it redirects to the login page. 2. It loads industries and projects from the Yard. 3. It restores the last agent run and opens the last page. 4. Clicks, typing and changes are caught by page-wide listeners that update the in-memory state and redraw the matching screen. 5. Generating a recipe creates a run on the agent server, follows its progress through a WebSocket with polling as a backup, and then loads the outputs. 6. Chat messages go to the agent when a successful run exists, otherwise to scripted replies.
inputs: Clicks, typing and selections on the page; the sign-in token; project lists from the Yard API; run status and results from the agent server.
outputs: Redrawn screens, chat messages, short pop-up notices, requests to the agent and Yard servers, and links to HTML, PDF and PowerPoint outputs.
risks: The admin password is kept in browser session storage and sent with feedback requests. Chat falls back to fixed scripted replies that sound like real edits. The redirect URL contains a hardcoded version string. Only lines 3651 to 4620 were supplied for review, so the first 3650 lines were not checked.
debug: Open the browser developer console; errors and warnings are logged with the step that failed. If the page keeps going to the login page, check the sign-in token. If progress stops, check whether the run status address responds and whether the WebSocket connects. If projects are missing, check the Yard export and the industry load step.
